## Introduction

**Partial Differential Equations (PDEs)** are equations that involve an unknown 
function of several variables and their partial derivatives.  PDEs are used 
to formulate many applied problems in physics, engineering and optimization 
including heat transfer, wave propagation, fluid flow and elasticity.  In this 
series of notes we will cover the fundamentals of PDEs including their 
classification, solution methods and applications.

The study of PDEs is quite complicated and draws on many areas of mathematics. 
It is recommended to have studied the following topics before tackling PDEs:

* Multivariate Calculus
* Ordinary Differential Equations
* Multidimensional Integration

Some additional topics that are helpful but not strictly necessary include:

* Measure Theory
* Functional Analysis

In making these study notes I have used the following resources:

1. Bright Side of Mathematics: Partial Differential Equations Series.
2. Lecture Notes by Prof. Viktor Grigoryan, Fall 2010, UC Santa Barbara.
3. Lecture Notes by Prof. Denis Labutin, Fall 2026, UC Santa Barbara.

## Partial Derivatives

First recall the following definition of a partial derivative from 
our study of multivariate calculus.

:::{.definition data-title="Partial Derivative"}

A **partial derivative** of a function $u:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ 
in variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ with repect to $j$-th variable 
is the derivative of $u$ with respect to $x_j$ while keeping all other 
variables fixed

$$
\partial_j u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_j}, \quad j = 1, 2, \ldots, n,
$$

also written as $D_j u$, $\partial_{x_{j}}$ or $u_{x_j}$.  

:::

We also write $\partial_j^k$ (or $D_j^k$) for the $k$-th partial derivative
with respect to the $j$-th variable.  

:::{.definition data-title="Multi-Index"}

A **multi-index** $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$ is an $n$-tuple of
non-negative integers.  The **order** of a multi-index is given by 
$\| \alpha \| = \alpha_1 + \ldots  + \alpha_n$.  We define

$$
D^\alpha
  = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \ldots \partial_n^{\alpha_n} 
  = \frac{\partial^{\| \alpha \|}}{\partial x_1^{\alpha_1} \ldots \partial x_n^{\alpha_n}}
$$

:::

:::{.example}

Consider the function $u(x,y) = 2x^2 + 4y^3 + 2xy$.  The partial derivative of 
$f$ with respect to $x$ and $y$ respectively are given by

$$
u_x = 4x + 2y, \quad u_y = 12y^2 + 2x.
$$

:::

## Partial Differential Equations

:::{.definition data-title="Partial Differential Equation"}

A **partial differential equation (PDE)** is an equation of an unknown 
function $u:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ (where typically 
$\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ open, $n \ge 2$) involving some 
partial derivative of $u$ 

$$
F(x, u(x), (D^\alpha u)(x)) = 0,
$$

where $F$ is a given function, $\alpha$ is a multi-index, and $D^\alpha u$ 
denotes the partial derivative of $u$ corresponding to the multi-index 
$\alpha$.

:::

A function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is a **(classical)** solution of a PDE if 
all partial derivatives appearing in the PDE are well-defined 
and the function $u$ satisfies the PDE at all points in $\Omega$. 

:::{.example}

A simple example of a PDE for function $u(x,y)$ written in different notations

$$
\begin{align*}
\cos (u) + 3u_{x} + 2u\cdot u_{xy} & = 0 \\
\cos (u) + 3 \partial_ x u + 2 u\cdot \partial _{xy} u & = 0\\
\cos (u) + 3D_x u + 2u\cdot D_x D_y u & = 0.
\end{align*}
$$

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Order of a PDE"}

The **order** of a PDE is the order of the highest partial derivative in 
the equation.  

:::

:::{.example}
The order of our last example is 2 since the highest order partial derivative 
is $u_{xy}$.
:::

## Differential Operators

To write PDEs compactly we think of differentiation as an operation applied to a
function.

:::{.definition data-title="Differential Operator"}
 
A **differential operator** of order $m$ is a map $L$ that takes a sufficiently
differentiable function $u$ to the function
$$
Lu(x)=\sum_{\|\alpha\|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\,(D^\alpha u)(x),
$$
where the $a_\alpha$ are given functions called the **coefficients**.

:::

:::{.example}

On functions $u(x,y)$ the operators 

$$
Lu=u_x+xu_y \quad \& \quad Mu=u_{xx}+3u_{xy}+2u_x+5u
$$

are differential operators of orders $1$ and $2$ with coefficients
$a_{(1,0)}=1,a_{(0,1)}=x$ and $a_{(2,0)}=1,a_{(1,1)}=3,a_{(1,0)}=2,a_{(0,0)}=5$
respectively. The Laplacian

$$
\Delta=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}^2
$$ 

is the second-order operator with all coefficients $1$ (see 
[[laplace-operator]]).

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Linear Operator"}

A map $L:V\to W$ between vector spaces is a **linear operator** if for all
$u,v\in V$ and scalars $c$
$$
L(cu+v)=cL(u)+L(v).
$$

:::

:::{.example}

We show the operator $Mu=u_{xx}+3u_{xy}+2u_x+5u$ above is linear. Differentiation
is linear, $\partial(cu+v)=c\,\partial u+\partial v$, and multiplying by a
function $a(x)$ is linear, so each term $a_\alpha D^\alpha u$ is linear in $u$,
and a sum of linear maps is linear. Directly,
$$
M(cu+v)=c\,u_{xx}+v_{xx}+3(cu_{xy}+v_{xy})+2(cu_x+v_x)+5(cu+v)=cMu+Mv.
$$

By contrast, $Nu=u_x+u^2$ is not linear since $N(2u)=2u_x+4u^2\neq2Nu$, and
neither is $Nu=u_x+1$ since $N(0)\neq0$.

:::

Every differential operator $Lu=\sum a_\alpha D^\alpha u$ whose coefficients
depend only on $x$ is linear. This is the case of interest in the next section.

## Linear and Nonlinear PDEs

:::{.definition data-title="Linear PDE"}

A PDE is **linear** of order $m$ if it can be written as
$$
Lu=\sum_{\|\alpha\|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\,(D^\alpha u)(x)=f(x),\qquad x\in\Omega,
$$
where $L$ is a linear differential operator and $a_\alpha$, $f$ are given
functions. A PDE which is not linear is called **nonlinear**.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Homogeneous PDE"}

A linear PDE is **homogeneous** if $f\equiv0$, that is, it can be written as
$$
Lu=0.
$$
Equivalently, every term contains the unknown function $u$ or one of its
derivatives. Otherwise the PDE is **inhomogeneous**.

:::

Linearity gives the important **superposition principle**: if $Lu_1=0$ and
$Lu_2=0$ then $L(c_1u_1+c_2u_2)=0$, so the solutions of a homogeneous linear PDE
form a vector space. If $u_p$ is any solution of $Lu=f$ then *all* solutions are
$u=u_p+u_h$ with $Lu_h=0$.

Nonlinear PDEs are divided according to how nonlinear the highest-order
derivatives are:

- **Semilinear:** the highest-order derivatives appear linearly with
  coefficients depending only on $x$, e.g. $\Delta u=u^3$.
- **Quasilinear:** the highest-order derivatives appear linearly but the
  coefficients may depend on $u$ and lower-order derivatives, e.g. Burgers'
  equation $u_t+uu_x=0$.
- **Fully nonlinear:** nonlinear in the highest-order derivatives, e.g. the
  eikonal equation $u_x^2+u_y^2=1$.

:::{.example}

Order and type of $u_t-u_{xx}+xu=0$: second order, linear homogeneous. Of
$u_t-u_{xx}+1=0$: second order, linear inhomogeneous ($f=-1$). Of
$u_t+u_{xxx}+\sqrt{1+u}=0$: third order, semilinear (hence nonlinear).

:::

## Classification of PDEs

There are two lenses through which to view PDEs: the mathematical structure
and the physical phenomena they model.

### Classification by Mathematical Structure

The classification below is for **second-order linear** PDEs (it extends to
quasilinear ones by freezing the coefficients at a given solution). Write
$$
Lu=\underbrace{\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}a_{ij}(x)\,u_{x_ix_j}}_{\text{principal part}}+\underbrace{\sum_ib_i(x)u_{x_i}+c(x)u}_{\text{lower-order terms}},
\qquad A=(a_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{n}\ \text{symmetric}.
$$
The **principal part** consists of the highest-order terms, which are the ones
that determine the qualitative behaviour. The type at a point $x$ depends on the
[[eigenvectors]] of $A(x)$:

1. **Elliptic** - all eigenvalues of $A$ are non-zero and have the same sign.
2. **Parabolic** - one eigenvalue of $A$ is zero and the rest are non-zero with
   the same sign.
3. **Hyperbolic** - one eigenvalue of $A$ has a different sign than the rest
   (and none is zero).

In two dimensions, the classification can be determined by the discriminant of
the principal part. For a second-order PDE in two variables $x$ and $y$ of the
form
$$
a u_{xx} + b u_{xy} + c u_{yy} + (\ \text{lower order terms}) = 0,
$$
the PDE is classified as follows:
$$
\begin{cases}
b^2 - 4ac < 0 & \text{elliptic} \\
b^2 - 4ac = 0 & \text{parabolic} \\
b^2 - 4ac > 0 & \text{hyperbolic}.
\end{cases}
$$

(This is the eigenvalue test for $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b/2\\b/2&c\end{pmatrix}$,
whose determinant is $ac-b^2/4$.) The type is tied to the existence of
*characteristic curves*, see [[pde-characteristics]].

The prototypical examples of each type of PDE are given in Table 1 below.

| Type | Prototypical Example | Typical Behavior |
|------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Elliptic | Laplace's Equation: $\Delta u = 0$, Poisson's Equation: $-\Delta u = f$.  | Equilibrium or steady state, boundary value problems, smooth solutions, every point influences each other.  |
| Parabolic | Heat Equation: $u_t = \Delta u$ | Smoothing, irreversible in time, infinite propagation speed, initial-boundary value problems. |
| Hyperbolic | Wave Equation: $u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u$ | Finite propagation speed, real characteristics, singularities travel, time-reversible. |

See [[laplace-equation]], [[heat-equation]] and [[wave-equation]].

### Classification by Physical Phenomena

Alternatively, PDEs can be classified by asking what a solution does as
time evolves.  A good way to see the distinction is to test each equation on a
plane wave $u=\exp (i(kx - \omega  t))$, which gives a dispersion relation
$\omega  = \omega (k)$.

| Phenomenon | Model Equation | Dispersion Relation | Observations |
|------------|----------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Transport (Advection) | $u_t + c u_x = 0$ | $\omega = ck$ | Profile moves rigidly at speed $c$: $u = f(x-ct)$. |
| Diffusion | $u_t = D u_{xx}$ | $\omega = -iDk^2$ | Modes decay like $\exp(-Dk^2t)$, so high frequencies die fastest and the profile smooths and spreads. |
| Wave Propagation | $u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}$ | $\omega = \pm ck$ | Two transport waves, profile moves rigidly at speed $c$: $u = f(x-ct) + g(x+ct)$. |
| Dispersion (Schroedinger) | $i u_t = -\frac{1}{2} u_{xx}$ | $\omega = \frac{1}{2} k^2$ | Modes rotate in the complex plane at different speeds, so the profile spreads and oscillates. |

See [[transport-equation]].
